quote.text: In every walk with nature, one receives far more than he seeks.
quote.author: John Muir

fun_fact.text: Hungarian shepherds bred the Puli dog with its distinctive corded coat that resembles dreadlocks. These intelligent herding dogs were so valued that a good Puli could cost a shepherd's entire year's salary! The cords naturally form as the dog matures and help protect them from harsh weather and wolf bites.

short_read.title: Why Do Hummingbirds Hum?
short_read.teaser: These tiny jewels of the bird world create their distinctive sound not with their voices, but with their incredible wings. Discover the fascinating science behind the hum and why these birds are engineering marvels of nature.

medium_read.title: The Secret Language of Flowers in Victorian Gardens
medium_read.teaser: In the 1800s, every flower carried a hidden message, from roses declaring love to lavender expressing devotion. This charming tradition transformed gardens into living letters and gave new meaning to every bouquet.

long_read.title: The Ancient Forests of the Olympic Peninsula
long_read.teaser: The temperate rainforests near Port Angeles are among the oldest and most remarkable ecosystems on Earth, where trees live for centuries and moss drapes like velvet curtains. National Geographic explores these cathedral-like groves that have witnessed hundreds of years of Pacific Northwest history.

port_angeles.title: Harbor Seal Pupping Season Wraps Up
port_angeles.description: September marks the end of harbor seal pupping season along the Strait of Juan de Fuca. By now, most of the adorable pups born this summer have learned to fish on their own and are exploring the waters near Port Angeles. You might spot them hauled out on rocks at low tide, resting between feeding sessions.

puzzle_1.question: A hummingbird's heart beats approximately ___ times per minute while in flight.
puzzle_1.correct_response: Exactly right, Barbara! That tiny heart works incredibly hard to power those amazing wings!
puzzle_1.close_response: You're very close! The answer is 1,200 beats per minute — that's about 20 times per second!
puzzle_1.wrong_response: The answer is 1,200 beats per minute! It's hard to imagine such a tiny heart beating so fast, but it's what gives hummingbirds their incredible flying abilities.
puzzle_1.learn_more_text: To put this in perspective, a human heart beats about 60-100 times per minute at rest. A hummingbird's metabolic rate is so high that they must eat constantly and enter a hibernation-like state called torpor at night to conserve energy.

puzzle_2.question: Which Hungarian word means 'hello' or 'goodbye' in an informal, friendly way?
puzzle_2.correct_response: Wonderful, Ildiko! Szia is such a warm, friendly greeting — perfect for friends and family!
puzzle_2.wrong_response: The answer is 'Szia'! It's one of the most common informal greetings in Hungarian, used with friends and people you know well. Köszönöm means 'thank you,' Igen means 'yes,' and Viszlát is a more formal goodbye.
puzzle_2.learn_more_text: Szia comes from the word 'szolga' meaning servant, originally meaning 'at your service.' Like many greetings around the world, it started as a formal phrase but became casual and friendly over time!

puzzle_3.question: Which famous explorer mapped much of the Pacific Northwest coast, including the waters near Port Angeles, in the 1790s?
puzzle_3.correct_response: That's right! Captain George Vancouver charted these waters in 1792, and the city of Vancouver is named in his honor. His detailed maps and journals documented the beauty of the Strait of Juan de Fuca and Puget Sound.
puzzle_3.wrong_response: The answer is Captain George Vancouver! He explored and mapped the Pacific Northwest coast in 1792, creating detailed charts of the waters you see from Port Angeles. Both Vancouver, British Columbia, and Vancouver, Washington are named after him.
puzzle_3.learn_more_text: Vancouver's expedition included the artist-botanist Archibald Menzies, who documented the region's incredible plants and wildlife. Their detailed records give us a window into what the Olympic Peninsula looked like over 230 years ago.
